topics: 🔟 Ten Generations — Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda on how far the guaranteed-flock exemption reaches
🐐 A Ewe That Gave Birth to a Goat — four ways to read Rabbi Meir's ruling
🧶 An Animal That 'Has Not Changed' — kilayim, tekhelet, tzaraat, and libations
👶 Twins With One Head Each — the new mishna on a ewe's simultaneous births
⚖️ Can Precision Ever Be Achieved? — the Gemara tests אפשר לצמצם against Temple law

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Resemblance, Generations, and Precise Measurement
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 17a–17b
overview.hebrewSource: רָחֵל שֶׁלֹּא בִּיכְּרָה וְיָלְדָה שְׁנֵי זְכָרִים, וְיָצְאוּ שְׁנֵי רָאשֵׁיהֶן כְּאַחַת
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf closes out the sugya on animals accepted from a gentile as a guaranteed investment (צֹאן בַּרְזֶל), debating exactly how many generations of offspring remain exempt from firstborn sanctity. It then returns to the mishna's ewe that gave birth to a goat-like creature, working through four different accounts of what Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis actually disputed — first-shearing wool, paternity concerns, or which ancestor's appearance controls firstborn status. A cluster of 'everyone agrees' rulings follows about wool, dye, leprosy marks, and libations from an animal or plant that has 'changed' from its natural kind. A new mishna then poses a ewe giving birth to twin males whose heads emerge simultaneously, launching a Gemara-wide investigation into whether two events — in Heaven's hands or in human hands — can ever coincide with true precision.

slides.title: 🔟 How Many Generations Stay Exempt?
slides.subtitle: Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda argue over the guaranteed-flock (צאן ברזל) mishna

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said offspring are exempt even until ten generations. But Rav Huna holds the first tanna never spoke of generations at all — so what does 'ten generations' mean?

lines.speaker: Rav Huna
lines.text: That phrase refers to the mishna's second case, where the Jew established the offspring in place of the mothers. There, the first tanna does descend to generations.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Come and hear an objection to Rav Yehuda: one who accepts tzon barzel from a gentile — the direct offspring are exempt, but offspring of offspring are not!

lines.speaker: Rav Yehuda
lines.text: I could say the mishna's phrase 'the offspring are exempt' refers to the offspring of the offspring, not the original animals' direct young.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Others report the mishna as 'they and their offspring are exempt' — that refutes Rav Huna!

lines.speaker: Rav Huna
lines.text: I could say 'they and their offspring' means the original animals and their direct young are exempt, but the offspring of that generation are obligated.

callout.label: Method:
callout.text: Each sage rereads the disputed wording of the mishna rather than concede — a recurring pattern of resolving apparent refutations.

slides.title: 🐐 What Was Rabbi Meir Really Ruling On?
slides.subtitle: Rav Oshaya's baraita: a ewe born to a goat, or a goat born to a ewe — Rabbi Meir obligates, the Rabbis exempt

boxes.title: Not About Wool
items: First guess: Rabbi Meir requires firstborn status only if offspring resembles its mother (Numbers 18:17) — so his ruling must concern first-shearing of wool instead
Objection: tough-fleeced lambs are exempt from first shearing (Job 31:20) — a goat-like fleece is tough
Rabba's fix: really about concern for the father's seed for slaughtering it and its offspring together

boxes.title: Firstborn — Mother or Grandmother?
items: Case: a ewe born to a ewe born to a goat (resembles mother, not grandmother)
Rabbi Meir: follow the mother's appearance — firstborn applies
Rabbis: follow the mother's mother's appearance — this is נִדְמֶה, exempt
Alt. case: ewe born to goat born to ewe — did its 'ovine nature return to its place'?

boxes.title: Rav Ashi — Partial Resemblance
items: Case: offspring has only some of its mother's characteristics
Rabbi Meir (= our mishna): firstborn status applies even with partial resemblance
Rabbis = Rabbi Shimon: requires head and majority of the body to resemble the mother

callout.label: Rabbi Yoḥanan's caveat:
callout.text: Even Rabbi Meir concedes the New Moon goat-offering must be the 'son of a female goat' since Creation — derived from the extra word 'one' (Numbers 28:15), or from Leviticus 22:27 excluding both diverse kinds and נִדְמֶה.

slides.title: 🧵 An Animal 'That Has Not Changed'
slides.subtitle: A chain of sages apply the same verbal analogy (from Deuteronomy 22:11's 'linen') across unrelated halakhot
rows: Wearing wool of a changed animal with linen
No flogging for kilayim — 'linen unchanged' means the wool, too, must be unchanged
A garment woven from such wool
Does not become impure with leprous marks (Leviticus 13:47)
A grapevine trellised over a fig tree
Its wine is unfit for libations (Leviticus 23:37, 'offering and libations')
Still valid — only the vine's scent changed; the flax's scent did not

callout.label: Pattern:
callout.text: 'Changed' is measured by a real, functional alteration (like altered scent), not merely by unusual growing conditions.

slides.title: 👶 Twins Whose Heads Emerge Together
slides.subtitle: New mishna: a ewe's first delivery is two males, both heads out at once

nodes.content: ❓ Who gets the firstborn — the owner or the priest?

columns.label: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
columns.content: Both go to the priest — 'the males shall be to the Lord' (Exodus 13:12) is plural

columns.label: The Rabbis
columns.content: Two events cannot coincide precisely — one truly preceded the other, so one lamb to the owner, one to the priest

columns.label: Rabbi Tarfon
columns.content: The priest chooses the better of the two lambs

columns.label: Rabbi Akiva
columns.content: Value is assessed between them; the second grazes until blemished, then the owner may eat it

nodes.content: ⚖️ Gifts of the priesthood (foreleg, jaw, maw) apply to the owner's lamb too — except Rabbi Yosei exempts it

callout.label: If one twin dies:
callout.text: Rabbi Tarfon: the survivor is divided; Rabbi Akiva: it stays with the owner, since the burden of proof is on the claimant. A male and a female together: the priest gets nothing at all.

slides.title: ⚖️ Can Two Things Ever Coincide Precisely?
slides.subtitle: The Gemara tests אֶפְשָׁר לְצַמְצֵם against cases across the Temple and beyond

steps.content: 1️⃣ School of Rabbi Yannai: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili holds even events in Heaven's hands (twin births) can coincide exactly — so human measurement certainly can. The Rabbis deny this for Heaven's hands — but what about human hands?
2️⃣ Proof attempt: the red line marking the altar's exact midpoint (Middot) — rejected, since the line is deliberately widened for safety
3️⃣ Proof attempt: the Torah gives exact measurements for Temple vessels and the altar — rejected, since 'do it as best you can' is all God requires
4️⃣ Rav Ketina: an impure oven split into two equal pieces leaves both impure, since exact division is impossible — Rav Kahana rejects this: earthenware has irregular indentations

5️⃣ Rabbi Eliezer's eglah arufah ruling: if a corpse is found exactly between two towns, both bring heifers — suggesting human measurement can be precise. The Gemara begins to reject this proof too, continuing onto 18a

callout.label: Open question:
callout.text: By the end of 17b, no proof for or against human precision (אפשר לצמצם בידי אדם) has survived unchallenged.

summary.principle: Firstborn and generational exemptions turn on precise definitions — how many generations, which ancestor's appearance controls, and whether two events can ever coincide with true precision.

flowSteps.content: 🔟 Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda reread the tzon barzel mishna to fix how many generations stay exempt
🐐 Rabbi Meir vs. Rabbis on the goat-like ewe: wool, paternity, or which ancestor's appearance decides firstborn status
🧵 A chain of sages: wool, tekhelet, tzaraat, and libations all require an animal or plant 'that has not changed'

columns.content: 👶 Twins with simultaneous heads: R' Yosei HaGelili gives both to the priest; the Rabbis split them
⚖️ Every proof for or against 'human precision' (אפשר לצמצם) is challenged and answered

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Uncertain simultaneity — whether in birth, measurement, or resemblance — is resolved by tracing the exact wording of the governing verse or mishna

quiz.q: According to Rav Huna, to which case of the tzon barzel mishna does Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's phrase 'even until ten generations' refer?
o: The case of the direct offspring only
The case where the Jew established the offspring in place of the mothers
A case not discussed in the mishna at all
The case of a gentile's firstborn animal
quiz.e: Rav Huna holds the first tanna does not normally speak of generations, so Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's remark must apply to the mishna's second case, where offspring were substituted for the mothers and generational descent is relevant.

quiz.q: In the baraita about a ewe that gave birth to a goat-like creature, what does Rabbi Meir's ruling concern according to Rav Ashi's interpretation?
o: Whether the wool may be used for tzitzit
An offspring that has only some, not all, of its mother's characteristics
Whether the priest may eat the offspring
The New Moon goat offering
quiz.e: Rav Ashi explains that Rabbi Meir's mishna-based position obligates firstborn status even when the offspring has only partial resemblance to its mother, while the Rabbis (Rabbi Shimon) require the head and majority of the body to resemble the mother.

quiz.q: What do Rabbi Aḥa bar Yaakov, Rav Pappa, and Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak all agree about wool from an animal that resembles a different species?
o: It may be eaten without concern
It is fit for the Temple altar
It cannot be used for kilayim liability, tekhelet, or become impure with tzaraat marks — because it counts as 'changed'
It automatically confers firstborn status
quiz.e: All three derive from the verbal analogy to unchanged linen that only wool from an animal 'that has not changed' (i.e., resembles its own kind) can trigger these halakhot; a nidmeh animal's wool is excluded from each.

quiz.q: In the new mishna, when a ewe's first two offspring emerge with both heads out at once, what does Rabbi Yosei HaGelili rule?
o: Both males belong to the owner
One belongs to the owner and one to the priest
Both males are given to the priest, based on the plural 'the males shall be to the Lord'
The owner must wait until one is blemished
quiz.e: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili reads Exodus 13:12's plural 'the males' as requiring both simultaneously-born males to go to the priest, since he holds two events can coincide precisely even in Heaven's hands.

quiz.q: What is the Gemara's rejection of Rav Ketina's proof from the impure oven split into two equal pieces (both remaining impure)?
o: The oven was never truly impure
Earthenware has irregular indentations, making an exactly even split especially difficult
The case has nothing to do with precise measurement
Ovens are not covered by the laws of tumah
quiz.e: Rav Kahana answers that earthenware vessels are unusual because their break points are uneven due to indentations, so this case cannot prove anything about whether precise division is generally possible.
